It is the converse direction of `IndependentUses`, fixed to one pair and one rest. It fails for complements and clashes. "Values the total service equally" is read as two things. The two services are the same satisfaction. And everything else is the same `rest`. The conclusion is a preference, not a choice. 70: Apodictic.TimePreference.valuation_reading_is_free (praxis : DatedFrame) (agent : praxis.Agent) (now : praxis.Time) (soon late : praxis.End) : TimePreference.SameByValuation praxis agent now soon late → ¬praxis.PrefersEnd agent now late soon**On the valuation reading, time preference's negative half is free.** Take any frame, agent and date. Take two ends that are the same satisfaction by valuation. Then the later is never preferred. No claim is carried: the signature has none. That is because the sentence was made true by what "same" was allowed to mean. The strict half is NOT free on this reading: that the sooner IS preferred. Take two ends, neither preferred to the other. The valuation reading counts them the same satisfaction. Time preference then asserts a preference that is not there. So on this reading the whole content of the claim is one thing: of two ends, one before the other and the sooner not yet past, the pair is never left unranked. That is comparability, and neither author argues for it.

67: Apodictic.TimePreference (praxis : DatedFrame) (agent : praxis.Agent) (now : praxis.Time) : Prop**Time preference** — of two ends that are the same satisfaction, the agent at `now` prefers the one attained sooner. This holds provided the sooner one is not already past. Source: Rothbard, *MES*, ch. 1, p. 15: "A fundamental and constant truth about human action is that man prefers his end to be achieved in the shortest possible time. Given the specific satisfaction, the sooner it arrives, the better." / "This is the universal fact of time preference." Mises, *Human Action*, ch. XVIII, §2: "Satisfaction of a want in the nearer future is, other things being equal, preferred to that in the farther distant future." / "Time preference is a categorial requisite of human action." Status: explicit-in-tradition as doctrine; our-reconstruction as a claim. Rothbard fixes "the same satisfaction" by the satisfaction it gives. Ice in summer and ice in winter "are not the same, but different goods" (*MES* pp. 15–16, n. 15). Read that way, the sentence cannot fail: whatever is preferred later was a different good. Mises sets ice aside on another ground, as "the case of perishable goods". Winter ice is "a good that loses its specific usefulness even if not consumed". Summer ice is "another good which requires a different process of production" (*Human Action*, ch. XVIII, §2). Neither is a fact about the ranking. Here `SameSatisfaction` is supplied apart from `Prefers`. So the claim constrains the ranking. An agent who prefers the same satisfaction later refutes it. The reading on which it cannot fail is built as the rejected encoding (`Apodictic.TimePreference.valuation_reading_is_free`). Carried by `Apodictic.TimePreference.less_durable_preferred` and by the interest theorems in `Apodictic.PureInterest`. Does not say: 1. Anything about ends that are not the same satisfaction. "Other things being equal" is carried whole by `SameSatisfaction`. A perishable good gives a pair that is not the same satisfaction. So do two enjoyments that cannot be had together (Mises's Carmen and Hamlet). So does unequal certainty of getting it. The claim is silent on each. It is silent on anticipation too. A pleasure put off brings the looking forward with it, from now until it comes. A pain got over with spares the waiting for it. Either way, the later option holds a satisfaction that begins now, and the earlier does not. That is the literature's own account: savouring is "positive utility derived from anticipation of future consumption", dread "negative utility resulting from contemplation of the future" (Loewenstein, *Economic Journal* 1987, p. 667). It counts as a diagnosis only where the anticipation is shown apart from the choice it explains. Inferred from the choice to wait, it is the valuation reading again. 2. Anything about bundles. Preferring a sooner bundle needs `DatedFrame.LiftsOverRest`. 3. Anything about ends already past at `now`. 4. That `Before` is transitive, irreflexive or total. The claim uses "sooner" only as a label on the pair. 5. How MUCH sooner is better. No rate, no discounting. 6. That the preference shows in any act. That bridge is `DemonstratedTimePreference`, of one act.

So he demonstrates no ranking of the umbrella at all. It is the scope of "unique goods" (*MES* p. 86) made explicit.

It is the bundle-level cousin of `IndependentUses`, fixed to one trade's holding. Nothing is said about any other holding the agent might rank. It fails for complements. A man who keeps a right shoe may rank (right shoe + left shoe) above (right shoe + hat). He may still rank a hat above a left shoe on its own. The left shoe's worth is in the pair. That may come through his own error, or through deception. Rothbard counts a deceived party's trade as not voluntary at all ("this is not an example of voluntary exchange, but of one-sided theft", *MES* p. 184). Under a threat it is worse. It is a field because the act alone does not fix it. The same handing-over is a trade or a robbery. Which one it is depends on what refusing would have cost. Shape: our-reconstruction. `kept` is read as the rest of the holding. A `Trade` whose given or received good is also among the kept describes no trade. Nothing rules that out, because no theorem in the library needs to. Rothbard assumes the two goods differ ("we implicitly assumed that it must be two different goods that are being exchanged", *MES* p. 95). For him it is a condition for an exchange to take place. No theorem in the library uses that either. So a `Trade` does not require it.

Say that when trading, the agent ranked the holding he chose above the one he gave up. Then he still does. It fails when he changes his mind. That is regret. Only this one pair is constrained. Nothing is said of the rest of his scale.
50: Apodictic.Allocation {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} (stock : Stock praxis agent time) : Type**An actual allocation** — what the agent does with the stock he holds at its time. It records the ends he serves with it, and nothing else. This is the object of the TEMPORAL reading of the law (`Apodictic.Temporal`). `AllocationPlan` assigns served ends to every sub-stock at once. That is the standing disposition the counterfactual reading needs. This structure instead records one allocation of one stock at one time. It is indexed by nothing: not by sub-stock, not by size. What the agent would have done with fewer units is not in it. It cannot be asked of it. Mises's history — "if the supply available increases from n–1 units to n units" — is then two of these at two times. It is not one plan read at two sizes. Field-shape claim (audit): `servesOnlyWhatItCan` is definitional, as for the plan. Putting a unit to an end the good is not believed able to serve is not an allocation of that good. Like the plan, an allocation is a thing over and above `Action`. An `Action` has one chosen end. A stock of several units serving several ends is several actions, or one action whose end is a bundle. The library does not say which, and no theorem asks.
48: Apodictic.ActsInOrder {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (allocation : Allocation stock) : Prop**Acts in order of urgency** — nothing serviceable and more urgent is passed over for something less urgent, in what the agent ACTUALLY does with the stock he holds. Say the agent serves an end. Say he prefers to it another end he believes the good can serve. Then he serves that end too. This is the actual-action twin of `ServedInOrder`. That claim is subjunctive: it is asserted of a plan over sub-stocks the agent may not hold. This one is asserted of one allocation of one stock at one time. The TEMPORAL reading of the law (`Apodictic.Temporal`) spends it in place of a standing plan. Source: Rothbard, *MES*, ch. 1, §5.B, p. 24, in the passage that narrates the acquisition of horses one by one: "The first horse will fulfill the most urgent wants that a horse can serve; this follows from the universal fact that action uses scarce means to satisfy the most urgent of the not yet satisfied wants". Mises, *Human Action*, ch. IV, §2, states the same agreement and gives its ground: "Every action is always in perfect agreement with the scale of values or wants because these scales are nothing but an instrument for the interpretation of a man's acting." Status: our-reconstruction. The words are Rothbard's. The claim is not quite his. Both authors deny that a value scale exists apart from the action it is read from. Mises: "The scale of value manifests itself only in real acting; it can be discerned only from the observation of real acting. It is therefore impermissible to contrast it with real acting and to use it as a yardstick for the appraisal of real actions" (ch. V, §4). Rothbard: "praxeology may deal with utilities only as deduced from the concrete actions of human beings" (p. 882). On their account the sentence holds of every act by interpretation. No act could contradict it. Here `PrefersEnd` is a ranking kept distinct from the allocation. So the claim constrains the act. Take an act that serves a lesser end while passing over a preferred end he believes the good can serve. That act refutes it. Only the ordering half of Rothbard's sentence is taken. Its "scarce means" half is not. Does not say: 1. Anything about sub-stocks the agent does not hold, or about any other time. In particular, nothing about how this allocation relates to one made at another time with a different stock. That relation, if any, is a theorem's to state and pay for. 2. That action reveals preference. This claim runs from the ranking to the act. The bridge from an act to a preference (`DemonstratedPreference`) is stated of trades only. Allocations are not trades. A bridge that read the ranking off the act would make this claim hold by construction. That is the authors' reading above. 3. That the ends a good can serve are comparable (`Stock.ComparableServiceable`). Nor anything about the order between two ends both served. 4. That the scale at this time bears on the scale at any other (constancy). Mises denies it: "value judgments are not immutable" (ch. V, §4). The library does not assert it as a claim. As a condition it appears once, for one pair of holdings in one trade (`Trade.RankingHolds`). Where the temporal reading would need it, the library exhibits the failure instead (`Apodictic.Model`). 5. How much is served. Not that every unit is used. Not that as many ends are served as the stock allows. An agent who serves nothing satisfies it. 6. Anything about ends the agent does not believe the good can serve. Passing those over is a matter of belief, not of this claim.

452: self.Agent → self.Time → Set self.End → Set self.End → Prop`Prefers agent time X Y`: at that time, the agent values the bundle of ends `X` above the bundle `Y`. This is the ranking behind the agent's choices. It is read as strict. But that reading is not built in: NO properties are imposed on this relation, strict or otherwise. A theorem that needs one says so. The ranking is kept apart from what the agent actually does. Three claims tie the two. Two run from an act to the ranking. `DemonstratedPreference` is stated of a trade. `DemonstratedTimePreference` is stated of an act across dates. One runs the other way, from the ranking to what he does with a stock. `ActsInOrder` is stated of an actual allocation. Each is asserted of the one trade, act or allocation a theorem is handed, never of every act. The relation ranges over SETS of ends rather than single ends. The tradition draws no line between an end and a composite of ends. The word "atomic" only ever means "not divided further by this action". That is the same relativity as the size of a unit of supply (*MES* p. 28). So there is ONE ranking, over bundles at whatever grain the problem has. An end in the ordinary sense is a bundle with one member (`PrefersEnd`). Independence of uses (`IndependentUses`) is bundle preference breaking down into preference between ends. Ranging over bundles is what lets it be a named hypothesis, instead of something the vocabulary quietly enforces. Shape claim (audit): a bundle is a `Set`, so it carries no multiplicity and no order.

41: Apodictic.DemonstratedPreference {praxis : ActionFrame} (trade : Trade praxis) : Prop**Demonstrated preference, in exchange** — the agent of a trade prefers the holding he chose to what refusing would have left him with. He prefers it at the time of trading. Both are counted by his beliefs at that time. This is the bridge from what an agent DOES to the ranking `Prefers`. The vocabulary otherwise keeps the two apart. It is asserted of the trade handed to a theorem, not of every trade. Source: Rothbard, *MES*, p. 307: "Any action demonstrates choice based on preference: preference for one alternative over others." p. 85, of exchange: "both people make it because they expect that it will benefit them; otherwise they would not have agreed to the exchange." p. 260: "We deduce the existence of a specific value scale on the basis of the real act". The doctrine is named "demonstrated preference" at p. 882, n. 8, citing Rothbard, *Toward a Reconstruction of Utility and Welfare Economics* (1956), pp. 224 ff. Status: explicit-in-tradition as doctrine; our-reconstruction as a claim. For Rothbard the scale is DEDUCED from the act (p. 260). So the sentence cannot fail: it defines what the scale says. Here `Prefers` exists apart from the act. So the claim constrains it. A trade made against the agent's own ranking at that moment refutes it. A slip can be such a trade. So can a compulsion he would disown. Does not say: 1. That the agent is better off afterwards. The comparison is made with his beliefs and his scale AT THE TRADE. It does not touch what the holding does for him later, or how he ranks it later (`Trade.BeliefsHold`, `Trade.RankingHolds`). 2. Anything about the two goods alone. It ranks whole holdings. The descent to "Y over X" is a theorem's to pay for (`Trade.SeparableFromRest`, `Trade.KeptServesOtherEnds`). 3. That the trade was voluntary. Under a threat the claim still holds: the victim prefers handing over to what refusing would cost. It then demonstrates nothing about the goods. `Trade.Voluntary` is what makes `refusal` the old holding. 4. Anything about other acts, other agents, or other times. It does not say that every act demonstrates preference.

168: Apodictic.Mises.ladder_for_every_served {praxis : ActionFrame} [DecidableEq praxis.End] {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (dominance : SwapDominant plan) (independent : praxis.IndependentUses agent time) (fewer more : Finset praxis.Means) (step : stock.OneMore fewer more) (kept : praxis.End) : kept ∈ plan.wouldServe fewer → ∀ added ∈ Mises.marginalEmployment plan fewer more, praxis.PrefersEnd agent time kept added**The ladder holds for EVERY end served at the smaller supply** — not only for the least urgent one. His sentence singles out "the least urgent or least painful among all those wants which could be removed by means of the supply n–1". This theorem drops the qualifier and keeps the conclusion. Whatever the extra unit adds is less urgent than ANYTHING the smaller supply serves. What it spends is `SwapDominant plan` — Rothbard's premise, and the whole of the warrant problem. It also spends independence of uses (`IndependentUses agent time`) and decidable equality of ends (`DecidableEq praxis.End`). It spends nothing Misesian at all.
167: Apodictic.Mises.LadderHolds {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) : Prop**Mises's ladder** — his statement of the law. It is written out as a target, so that what proves it, and from what, is legible. VII, §1). It is a `def` of a Prop, not a theorem, and deliberately so. It is reached twice below, from two different premise sets. `ladder_holds` derives it from Rothbard's premise. `ladder_from_order` derives it from Mises's own bridge. Which premises each spends is on each theorem's signature.
166: Apodictic.Mises.LeastUrgentServed {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (subStock : Finset praxis.Means) (want : praxis.End) : Prop**Least urgent among those served** — Mises's "the least urgent or least painful among all those wants which could be removed by means of the supply n–1". It says of a given end that nothing else served at that sub-stock ranks below it. It is stated of an end the law quantifies over. It is never asserted to exist. Whether such an end exists at all is a separate question. That question cannot be answered without saying more about `Prefers` than the library assumes. Inside the law it enters as a hypothesis on that end, not as a derived object. That is the first place the two routes visibly differ. Rothbard's derivation never needs a minimum. It compares two named steps. Mises's sentence names a minimum.
165: Apodictic.Mises.marginalEmployment {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (fewer more : Finset praxis.Means) : Set praxis.End**Mises's marginal employment** — the ends served at the larger supply and not at the smaller. VII, §1). It is stated as the DIFFERENCE of two counterfactual allocations at one time. That is what "other things being equal" asks for. It restates `marginalEnds` (in `Apodictic.MarginalUtility`) deliberately, because `Apodictic.Mises` does not import `Apodictic.MarginalUtility` or `Apodictic.Urgency`. That the two coincide is a theorem for a module importing both, not an `import` here. It is a definition, not a claim. Mises introduces it as a definition ("We call that employment ..."). He prefaces it with the remark that establishing it does not transcend praxeological reasoning.

It has the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value. That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`. Example: ``` example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop) (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b := Eq.subst h1 h2 example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop) (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b := h1 ▸ h2 ``` The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`. 145: Classical.choice.{u} {α : Sort u} : Nonempty α → α**The axiom of choice**. `Nonempty α` is a proof that `α` has an element, but the element itself is erased. The axiom `choice` supplies a particular element of `α` given only this proof. The textbook axiom of choice normally makes a family of choices all at once, but that is implied from this formulation, because if `α : ι → Type` is a family of types and `h : ∀ i, Nonempty (α i)` is a proof that they are all nonempty, then `fun i => Classical.choice (h i) : ∀ i, α i` is a family of chosen elements. This is actually a bit stronger than the ZFC choice axiom; this is sometimes called "[global choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_global_choice)". In Lean, we use the axiom of choice to derive the law of excluded middle (see `Classical.em`), so it will often show up in axiom listings where you may not expect. You can use `#print axioms my_thm` to find out if a given theorem depends on this or other axioms. This axiom can be used to construct "data", but obviously there is no algorithm to compute it, so Lean will require you to mark any definition that would involve executing `Classical.choice` or other axioms as `noncomputable`, and will not produce any executable code for such definitions.
144: Apodictic.marginalEnds {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (fewer more : Finset praxis.Means) : Set praxis.End**Marginal utility of a one-unit step**, from `fewer` to `more`, in Rothbard's own sense. It is the ends the extra unit adds. These are the same ends that would be given up if it were lost. "The marginal utility of the supply is the end that must be given up as the result of a loss of the unit" (*MES* p. 27); "he gives up the least urgent of the wants which the larger stock would have satisfied" (p. 25). It is a set of ends rather than a single end, because nothing here assumes that exactly one end drops. Determinacy of the drop is not among the law's premises. It is a `Set` rather than a `Finset` for a mechanical reason. Subtracting one `Finset` from another requires being able to decide when two ends are the same end. An arbitrary frame does not give us that. Reaching for `Classical` would put `Classical.choice` on the manifest for no praxeological reason at all. It is a definition, not a claim. Rothbard introduces it as a definition ("is called", "is known as"). What licenses calling this the utility of the *unit* is imputation of value from ends back to means: "actors value means strictly in accordance with their valuation of the ends that they believe the means can serve" (p. 19). It is indexed by the step rather than by a size. The reason is that which ends a unit adds can depend on which units are already on hand, unless interchangeability of units (`plan.Homogeneous`) holds.
142: Apodictic.urgency_principle {praxis : ActionFrame} [DecidableEq praxis.End] {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (dominance : SwapDominant plan) (independent : praxis.IndependentUses agent time) (fewer more : Finset praxis.Means) (step : stock.OneMore fewer more) (kept : praxis.End) : kept ∈ plan.wouldServe fewer → ∀ lost ∈ plan.wouldServe more, lost ∉ plan.wouldServe fewer → praxis.PrefersEnd agent time kept lost**The urgency principle** (Rothbard), stated as a loss. Suppose the agent had `more` units and drops to `fewer`, one unit fewer (`stock.OneMore fewer more`). Every end he would still serve at `fewer` is preferred to every end he has to abandon on the way down. The loss falls on the least urgent want. It is one application of `served_over_unserved`. An abandoned end is one the good can serve and the plan does not serve at `fewer`. Beyond supplying that much, the fact that `more` is exactly one unit larger does no work here.
141: Apodictic.insert_sdiff_self_of_mem {α : Type} [DecidableEq α] {bundle : Set α} {want : α} (h : want ∈ bundle) : bundle = insert want (bundle \ {want})Taking a member out of a set and putting it straight back leaves the set alone. 134: Apodictic.Stock.NoNewUses {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {earlierTime laterTime : praxis.Time} (earlier : Stock praxis agent earlierTime) (later : Stock praxis agent laterTime) : Prop**The good is believed to serve no new use** — whatever the good is believed to serve at the later moment, it was believed to serve at the earlier one. It is about BELIEF about the good, not about the scale of values. Between the two moments the man learns no new use for the good. The condition is there so that the want the added unit goes to was on the earlier scale at all. Where he does learn one, the earlier-judged ladder is silent. Does not say that the good's uses stay the same. A use believed in earlier may be dropped later. It says nothing about the scale at either moment. Then praxeology would assert that no such agent exists. This frame would then be a counter-example to the claim, not a gap in the theorem's reach.
132: Apodictic.served_over_unserved {praxis : ActionFrame} [DecidableEq praxis.End] {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (dominance : SwapDominant plan) (independent : praxis.IndependentUses agent time) (subStock : Finset praxis.Means) (onHand : subStock ⊆ stock.units) (served : praxis.End) : served ∈ plan.wouldServe subStock → ∀ unserved ∈ stock.serves, unserved ∉ plan.wouldServe subStock → praxis.PrefersEnd agent time served unserved**Served over unserved** — the workhorse. It is more than Rothbard says. It sets a served end against ANY unserved end the good could serve, not only against the one the next unit would reach. It needs the hypothesis of independence of uses (`IndependentUses agent time`). That hypothesis is what carries a preference between two bundles down to a preference between two ends. How the proof goes. Swap the `served` want for the `unserved` one, and the plan beats the result. The served bundle is that one want together with the rest (`insert_sdiff_self_of_mem`). So the two bundles differ in exactly one place. Independence of uses reads the preference between those two wants off that.
131: Apodictic.Temporal.ladder_judged_earlier {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {earlierTime laterTime : praxis.Time} {earlier : Stock praxis agent earlierTime} {later : Stock praxis agent laterTime} (before : Allocation earlier) (after : Allocation later) (order : ActsInOrder before) (comparable : earlier.ComparableServiceable) (noNewUses : earlier.NoNewUses later) : Temporal.Ladder before after earlierTime**The ladder, judged on the earlier scale** — a theorem, from a claim about actual action and two situational conditions. What it does NOT spend, as the signature shows: - Nothing about the later allocation beyond membership. - Nothing about the supply having grown. `Stock.Grows` is not a hypothesis. Added as one, it fails the unused-argument linter. - Nothing about the order of the two times. - Nothing about the later scale. The argument is Mises's. The added want was serviceable and unserved before. Had it been more urgent than something served, acting in order would have served it. Mises's minimality qualifier is idle here, as on both counterfactual routes. `least` need only have been served. So this is the ladder as a statement about the EARLIER allocation. 130: Apodictic.ActionFrame.IndependentUses (praxis : ActionFrame) (agent : praxis.Agent) (time : praxis.Time) : Prop**Independence of uses** — a condition on the situation, NOT a universal claim. It fails where uses are complementary: where B is worth having only alongside A. It is named here so that the theorems that need it carry it as a hypothesis. It is also named so that a reader can point at it where it does not hold. This is NOT a premise Rothbard spends. He ranks wants against each other directly. He ranks them off a scale that is already ranked (*MES* pp. 25–26, Figure 3). He never argues from bundles at all. This condition is what OUR decomposition costs. Where he makes one fused claim, we make a claim about bundles (`SwapDominant`) plus this condition. His wording never has to face complementarity. Once the pieces are pulled apart, complementarity lands here. To assert this condition rather than hypothesize it would be to assert that complementarity never happens.

That holds for ANY two one-unit steps reaching those sizes. The two steps need not have a single unit in common. Interchangeability of units (`plan.Homogeneous`) is needed exactly once. It is needed to say that the plan at the `n` units below the second step is the same as the plan at the `n` units of the first. Without it the two steps could not be compared at all. Here too only half of the marginality hypothesis is used. The unused half is destructured as `_notNeeded` in the proof. That is a proof-local name, not a binder in the statement. Every binder this theorem lists is used.
119: Apodictic.BuysMoreThanItsParts {praxis : MoneyFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {now : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis.toActionFrame agent now} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (sum : Finset praxis.Means) : Prop**Buys more than its parts** — a condition on the situation, NOT a claim. Every strict part of `sum` would buy other ends than the whole does. So the plan has a use for every unit of the sum. It fails for a sum larger than anything the agent would spend or hold it on.
118: Apodictic.RankedAlikeNowOf {praxis : MoneyFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {now : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis.toActionFrame agent now} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (spend : praxis.Time) (promise lesser : Finset praxis.Means) : Prop**Ranked alike now, of one comparison** — a condition on the situation, NOT a claim. Take the date `spend`, when the agent would spend the two sums. Suppose he then ranks what `promise` would buy above what `lesser` would buy. Then he ranks them so at `now` too. His valuation of these two purchases does not change in between. Mises: "If the valuations change, acting must change also" (*Human Action*, ch. V, §4). It fails for the man who now prefers to be repaid less. He prefers it because of what he would do with more.
116: Apodictic.MoneyFrame : Type 1A dated frame with money and the cost of holding it.
114: Apodictic.MoreMoneyPreferredWhenSpent {praxis : MoneyFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {now : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis.toActionFrame agent now} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) (spend : praxis.Time) : Prop**More money is preferred when it is spent** — take two sums of money, the one part of the other. Both are free to hold, and they would buy different ends. Take `spend`, the date the agent would spend them. At that date he prefers what the larger would buy to what the smaller would buy. It is asserted of one plan for one stock. It is asserted only of sums whose every unit is money and which cost nothing to hold. It is subjunctive, like the plans it is asserted of: it speaks of sums the agent may not hold. The plan says what he WOULD buy with a sum. He would buy it at `spend`, by his valuations then. The claim ranks the purchase there. Two further things are conditions, each on the theorem that needs it: - That he ranks it so at `now` too is the condition `RankedAlikeNowOf`. - That the larger sum would buy something else is the condition `BuysMoreThanItsParts`. Source: Rothbard, *MES* p. 379: "[T]o both present money and future money there applies the general rule that more of a good will have greater utility than less of it." Mises, *Human Action*, ch. VII, §1: "what satisfies more is preferred to what gives smaller satisfaction". Status: explicit-in-tradition as doctrine; the narrow form is our-reconstruction. Rothbard states a general rule, of every good. Known cases refute it as stated: - A holding taxed at more than its whole value makes more of a good worse than less. So, at small scale, does any storage or custody cost. - A sum beyond anything the agent would spend or hold it on would buy nothing more. - Take a man whose valuations change between now and the spending. He now prefers less cash at hand, because of what he would buy with it later (`Apodictic.Model.Impulse`). So the claim is cut to money, to sums free to hold, to purchases that differ, and to the date of spending. Each failure is a named condition. Carried by `Apodictic.PureInterest.present_sum_preferred_to_less` and the loan theorems built on it. Does not say: 1. Anything about his valuations at any date but `spend`. That they agree with his valuations now is a condition, not the claim. 2. That every sum in the plan is spent at the one date `spend`, or which date that is. `spend` is supplied with the plan. 3. That an extra unit would always buy something else. 4. Anything of goods that are not money, or of sums that cost something to hold. 5. How much more is preferred. No rate. 6. Anything of two sums neither of which is part of the other. That two sums of the same size would buy the same is the condition `AllocationPlan.Homogeneous`. 7. That the agent's preferences chain. Transitivity is the condition `ActionFrame.TransitiveOn`, on one chain. 8. Anything about acts. It ranks what sums would buy. The bridge to a trade is `DemonstratedPreference`.

So where a theorem needs the split, the split is this claim. Source: Mises, *Human Action*, ch. 10: Apodictic.AllocationPlan {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} (stock : Stock praxis agent time) : TypeThe agent's plan for the stock. Take each `subStock`, each set of units he might have. The plan gives the ends he WOULD serve with exactly those units, at the stock's single time. The plan is something new, over and above `Action`, and it has to be. A single act of allocating cannot tell the served ends apart from one another. They all sit inside the one package chosen. So what the law of marginal utility rests on is not action at all. The plan is a separate thing, and no act of the agent's exhibits it. The plan is indexed by WHICH units, not by how many. To say it depends only on the number of them is to say the units are interchangeable. That is not built in here. It is the named condition `Homogeneous`, assumed only where a theorem needs it. Field-shape claim (audit): `servesOnlyWhatItCan` is the one condition left in the plan's fields. It is definitional. Take a plan that puts a unit to an end the good is not believed able to serve. That is not a coherent plan. It is not a situation that might obtain. One unit to one end is NOT here, and is nowhere: no theorem needs it. Rothbard assumes it, and says he is assuming it. He writes "each unit of means is capable of serving one of the ends". He introduces it with "We assume for simplicity" (*MES* pp. 25–26). The ordering the law asserts turns out not to want it. Where an extra unit adds no new end, the law is silent. That costs nothing.
0: Apodictic.SwapDominant {praxis : ActionFrame} {agent : praxis.Agent} {time : praxis.Time} {stock : Stock praxis agent time} (plan : AllocationPlan stock) : Prop**Swap dominance** — the agent's plan beats every one-swap alternative to it. Take any sub-stock of the units on hand. Take the ends the agent would serve with it. Now make one swap. Drop a `served` end. Put in its place an `unserved` one: an end the good could have served but the plan left out. The claim is that the agent prefers the bundle he would have served to the swapped bundle. It is asserted of one given plan. It is subjunctive throughout. It speaks of sub-stocks the agent may not hold, and of swaps he does not make. Source: Rothbard, *MES*, ch. 1, §5.B, pp. 24–27 (Mises Institute ed.): "action uses scarce means to satisfy the most urgent of the not yet satisfied wants" (p. 24). The counterfactual framing is Rothbard's own ("suppose ... faced with the necessity of giving up one horse"; "he gives up the least urgent of the wants which the larger stock would have satisfied", p. 25). It is backed by the reallocation argument (p. 27: "follows from the defined interchangeability of units and from disregard of past events"). Mises, *Human Action*, ch. VII.1. Status: explicit-in-tradition as doctrine. Two things are our-reconstruction: the one-swap form, and the pulling apart of the two halves below. Rothbard's premise fuses two claims in one sentence. One is that ACTION employs the means. The other is that the wants served are "the most urgent of the not yet satisfied wants" (*MES* p. 24). This claim keeps the ordering half. It states it subjunctively, over what the agent WOULD serve. The subjunctive is Rothbard's own. His derivation compares a stock of six with a stock of five. It asks which want "the larger stock would have satisfied" (p. 25). No single actual allocation delivers that comparison. The action half is dropped, not answered. Nothing here bridges an act to a preference. A tension remains, and it is Rothbard's own. It is not that this claim reaches stocks the agent does not hold. That reach is his (see *Anything about units not on hand*, below). It is that the claim attributes a STANDING disposition. The plan is one object, at one time. It assigns served ends to every sub-stock at once. That is a value scale formulated in advance of the choices it covers. It is the thing Rothbard says is not needed. He holds that praxeology "may deal with utilities only as deduced from the concrete actions of human beings" (*MES* p. 882 n. 8). Inside this very chapter he writes that "value scales do not exist in a void apart from the concrete choices of action". He introduces those words with "It must be reiterated". He adds that "there is no need for him to formulate hypothetical value scales" (*MES* p. 33). His actor needs no scale in advance. The scale is revealed choice by concrete choice as he goes. This claim gives him one up front. Yet on that same page he exempts this law from the restriction. He does it in a subordinate clause, without argument. Choices cannot be predicted "except that they will follow the law of marginal utility, which was deduced from the axiom of action". So the one thing that may be said in advance about the choices is that they follow the law. That is what licenses attributing the standing plan this claim is asserted of. And that plan is the premise the law is derived from. The warrant for the premise is the conclusion. The circle is in the WARRANT, not in the proof. Nothing in the Lean is circular. `marginal_utility` derives the law from this claim. This claim is asserted, never proved. What is circular is Rothbard's licence for asserting it. It is asserted of ONE plan, not of every plan of that shape. That is not a hedge. Given one plan, a rival can always be defined. So a claim about all such plans could be refuted just by building one. Asserted of the single plan a theorem is handed, there is no such rival to build. Whether a rival one swap away could also be swap-dominant then becomes a theorem (`no_rival_swap_dominant`, `Apodictic.Urgency`). It is not a premise. Does not say: 1. Anything about actual action. No bridge from action to preference is part of this claim. 2. Anything about alternatives that differ by more than one swap. 3. Anything about independence of uses. That is the theorems' hypothesis `IndependentUses`. 4. Anything about units not on hand. The plan speaks only of sub-stocks of the units on hand (`subStock ⊆ stock.units`). The reach over stocks the agent does not hold is Rothbard's own, in both directions. He builds the law upward over stocks the actor lacks: the second unit, then the third "added to a stock of two units" (*MES* pp. 23–24). He also takes it downward, six horses to five (p. 25). Holding none of a good is no obstacle either: "If the actor has no units of some goods in his possession, this does not affect the principle" (p. 32). The hypothetical scales he refuses on the next page are a different thing. They are scales for a wholly different multi-good endowment, (3X, 4Y, 2Z) against (6X, 8Y, 5Z). Inside the actual stock he permits "adding and subtracting" units of it (p. 33). The line between the two is anchored to the stock the agent has. It is not drawn at some distance from it. It is closed under the single-unit steps he iterates himself: first horse, then second, then third. Taken downward from a stock, those steps reach every sub-stock of it. So quantifying over all of `subStock ⊆ stock.units` covers that region exactly. It is not a reach beyond his text. Where this claim does depart from him is in INDEXING, not in reach. It speaks of arbitrary sub-stocks where he speaks of sizes. The gap between the two is interchangeability. He assumes it throughout. This claim does not: interchangeability is the hypothesis `Homogeneous`. Stated without that assumption, the claim distinguishes cases he never had to tell apart. 5. Anything about interchangeability of units. That two sub-stocks of the same size would serve the same ends is the hypothesis `Homogeneous`. It is no part of this claim. 6. That such a plan exists. Nor that it is unique without further properties of `Prefers`.
